newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Progress seen in Swiss hunt for Holocaust accounts.
newsitem.headline: Progress seen in Swiss hunt for Holocaust accounts.

text.p: Swiss banks, accused by Jewish groups of sitting on the wealth of Holocaust victims, have apparently made progress in tracking down some missing funds that have gone unclaimed for decades.

Banking ombudsman Hanspeter Haeni on Friday called a news conference for November 12 to discuss the status of the search he is coordinating on behalf of some 1,000 claimants seeking assets their relatives may have put in secretive Swiss banks.
He declined to give any details, but referred to his previous comment that he was "convinced we can prove that the search process works".

"When the cases are prepared, they will be presented to the public," he told Reuters, adding he had already informed people involved. He said he would not name any bank account holders or banks, but would give general examples at the news conference.

The World Jewish Congress this week dismissed Haeni's effort to find the assets of Holocaust victims as a "cruel farce" and said not a single penny has been returned to survivors or their relatives after a year-long probe.

"After 2,000 inquiries and 1,000 formal claims, the Swiss ombudsman has returned not a cent. He has rejected every claimant for a year. This is a cruel farce perpetuated on Holocaust survivors by the Swiss banking industry," WJC vice president Kalman Sultanik said in New York.
A U.S. lawsuit by Holocaust survivors seeks $20 billion in assets, a figure Swiss officials dismiss as wildly exaggerated.

Haeni said he had circulated three lists to banks in May, July and September that contained the names of potential account holders. The first list alone was 70 pages long and had six potential account holders per page.
Banks then had two months to search their records, not just by the customer's name, but also by the names of relatives.

If they found a match, they could turn to Haeni's office to get forms filled out by applicants. It was then up to banks to get in touch with claimants. If he did not hear back from banks, he informed claimants of this "negative information".

A separate panel agreed by Swiss bankers and Jewish groups in May and headed by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker is also hunting for lost Holocaust funds. It is set to hire auditors soon to pore over banks' records.

In addition, parliament is set to give final approval in December to a commission of historians empowered to lift banking secrecy in limited cases as they conduct a sweeping review of Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre.
Thir goal is to produce a historical verdict on whether neutral Switzerland cynically profited from World War Two.

In tearful testimony at hearings called by U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, Holocaust survivors have described being stonewalled by Swiss banks, at times being asked for death certificates for relatives killed in Nazi concentration camps.
The Weltwoche weekly said such charges probed "what in the end is the sorest spot in our self-defence front" and had triggered an international camapign against Switzerland.
"It does not matter at all any more how justified this campaign is," it wrote.

"It is enough that no one in this country enjoys the respect and backing to put forward effectively a position in public discourse with foreign accusers and domestic questioners, either to reject the charges or to prove credibly that Switzerland is ready to lay bare its past, warts and all."
